summary: Japan grants visa-free entry of up to 90 days to citizens of around 70 countries and regions, offers an official eVisa for several other nationalities, and encourages all arrivals to pre-register immigration and customs details on the free Visit Japan Web service.

notes: Duty-free allowance: 200 cigarettes and 3 bottles (about 760 ml each) of alcohol per adult.
Many common medications (e.g. Those containing pseudoephedrine or codeine above set limits) are restricted. Check import rules and obtain a Yunyu Kakunin-sho certificate where needed.

payments.text: Cards and IC/QR payments are widespread in cities, but many small restaurants, shrines, rural shops and some ticket machines remain cash-only — always carry some yen.

safety.text: Japan is one of the safest countries in the world for travelers, with very low crime. Follow local guidance on earthquakes and typhoons.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Japan Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: Spring (March–May, cherry blossoms) and fall (October–November, foliage) offer the most pleasant weather; summer is hot and humid with typhoon risk.

idp.text: Japan is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Geneva, 1949), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3)

driving.text: Japan is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Japan yet.

tips.text: The only official Japan eVisa site is evisa.mofa.go.jp. Third-party sites charging extra "service fees" are unnecessary and sometimes fraudulent.
Register on Visit Japan Web (vjw-lp.digital.go.jp) before flying. It is free and its QR codes noticeably speed up immigration and customs.
Japan strictly bans some medications that are common elsewhere (e.g. Certain ADHD stimulants and high-dose pseudoephedrine products). Check the health ministry's rules before packing medicine.
Keep cash on hand: rural areas, small eateries and many temples do not take cards. 7-Eleven and post-office ATMs reliably accept foreign cards.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Japan?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can stay in Japan visa-free for up to 90 days for tourism or business meetings. They only need a passport valid for the whole stay and, ideally, a Visit Japan Web registration to speed up arrival.

faq.question: Who can use the Japan eVisa and what does it cost?
faq.answer: The official Japan eVisa at evisa.mofa.go.jp issues single-entry short-term visas for eligible nationalities and residents (Indian, Filipino and Vietnamese tourists among them, depending on where they apply). The fee matches the paper visa: about 3,000 JPY for single entry; multiple-entry embassy visas cost about 6,000 JPY.

faq.question: What is Visit Japan Web and is it mandatory?
faq.answer: Visit Japan Web (vjw-lp.digital.go.jp) is the government's free online service for pre-registering immigration and customs declarations. It is optional — paper forms still exist — but the QR codes it generates make arrival much faster, so registering before your flight is recommended.

faq.question: Can Chinese citizens visit Japan without a visa?
faq.answer: Japan has restored short-term visa exemption for Chinese citizens for stays of up to 30 days. Because this policy was reinstated recently and conditions may be adjusted, Chinese travelers should confirm the current rules with a Japanese embassy before booking.

faq.question: Can I extend a 90-day visa-free stay in Japan?
faq.answer: Generally no. Most visa-exempt visitors must leave within 90 days. Citizens of a few countries with 6-month arrangements (including the UK, Germany, Ireland, Switzerland and Mexico) can apply at a regional immigration bureau in Japan to extend up to 6 months in total.
